q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM (SELECT DISTINCT * FROM VIEWS) A GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(ARTICLE_ID) >1 ORDER BY ID
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM (SELECT DISTINCT * FROM VIEWS) A GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(ARTICLE_ID) >1 ORDER BY ID
counterexample: INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, 201, '2023-01-01'); INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (2, 102, 201, '2023-01-01');
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 groups by VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID, while Q2 groups by VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID, and all other columns in the VIEWS table. This difference in grouping can lead to different results when applying the HAVING clause.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have multiple views by the same viewer on the same date, but with different articles. Q1 should return this viewer, while Q2 should not, due to the additional grouping by ARTICLE_ID in the subquery.
